concept: pandas DataFrames organize tabular data. Boolean filters select rows; groupby aggregates them at a chosen grain.
example:
import pandas as pd
orders = pd.DataFrame({"customer": [1, 1, 2], "amount": [500, 300, 600]})
result = (orders.loc[orders["amount"] >= 300]
          .groupby("customer", as_index=False)
          .agg(revenue=("amount", "sum"), order_count=("amount", "size")))
print(result)
breakdown: loc applies a row filter before aggregation.
groupby creates one group per customer.
agg assigns names to summed revenue and row counts.
as_index=False leaves customer as a regular column.
practice: Modify the code to keep only orders with amount > 400 and calculate average amount per customer.
takeaways: Filter order changes results: before grouping filters rows; after grouping filters groups.

deep_dive.heading: Keep the aggregation grain explicit
paragraphs: A filtered DataFrame retains only rows satisfying a boolean mask. Use parentheses around each comparison when combining masks with & or |.
Groupby collapses the original row-level records into the chosen grouping keys. The as_index=False option returns keys as ordinary columns, which often simplifies downstream joins.
Validate the sum of group totals against the filtered input sum to catch dropped rows or unexpected missing grouping keys.
deep_dive.code:
active = orders.loc[(orders["status"] == "paid") & (orders["amount"] > 0)].copy()
by_customer = active.groupby("customer_id", as_index=False, dropna=False).agg(
    revenue=("amount", "sum"),
    order_count=("order_id", "nunique")
)
assert abs(by_customer["revenue"].sum() - active["amount"].sum()) < 1e-8
